office.title: Indiana State Senator
office.summary: Members of the Indiana Senate write and vote on state laws as part of the Indiana General Assembly. The Senate has 50 members, each representing one district for a four-year term; about half the seats are elected every two years [1].
duties: Introduces and votes on state legislation as one of the two chambers of the Indiana General Assembly [1].
Must be at least 25 years old when taking office and have lived in the district for at least a year, under Article 4 of the Indiana Constitution [1].

incumbent.name: Ron Alting
incumbent.summary: Sen. Ron Alting, first elected in 1998 and chair of the Senate Public Policy Committee, is seeking another term [3].
record: Committees: The Senate Republican caucus lists him as chair of Public Policy and a member of Insurance and Financial Institutions [3].

2025: Voted against SB 1, the 2025 property-tax law, saying it was 'not a solution that provides meaningful tax relief for Hoosiers' and that relief should not become an excuse for growth in local income taxes [4].

Dec. 2025: Supported the mid-decade congressional redistricting proposal, which the Senate defeated; IPM reported he has at times voted against his party's majority, including on the 2022 near-total abortion ban bill [5].

2026 session: According to the Senate Republican caucus, he authored a bill banning vaping products made in foreign adversarial nations such as China, signed March 12 and effective July 1, and a bill coupling Indiana's tax code to federal 'no tax on tips' and 'no tax on overtime' provisions that passed the Senate 47–1 on Jan. 28 [3].

race_context: The Senate Republican caucus describes District 22 as Carroll County and portions of Tippecanoe County [3].

Republican primary (May 5, 2026): Alting 4,954 (59.1%) over Richard Bagsby 3,424 (40.9%); Democratic primary: Natasha Baker 3,554 (62.1%) over Marlena Edmondson 2,045, per Wikipedia's results compilation [6].
Trump endorsed Alting in March 2026; primary challenger Bagsby, who criticized Alting's voting record, had the backing of Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith [5].

In an Oct. 1, 2026 Journal & Courier Q&A, both candidates opposed shifting the tax burden from property taxes to local income taxes; they differed on the gas tax, with Alting favoring removing the sales tax on gas and Baker favoring reinstating the gas tax to fund roads [4].
No debate or forum between the candidates was found in available coverage.

candidates.summary: Ron Alting is the incumbent Republican, first elected in 1998 and a former Lafayette City Council president, who chairs the Senate Public Policy Committee [3].
background: According to the Senate Republican caucus, he is a Purdue University graduate, a business development leader at Trane, a major in the Indiana Guard Reserve, and was Lafayette City Council president from 1995 to 1998 [3].
path_to_ballot: Won the May 5, 2026 Republican primary with 59.1% over Richard Bagsby, per Wikipedia's results compilation [6].

items: He said he voted against SB 1 in 2025 and prioritizes local spending transparency, flexibility such as shared services, and safeguards against excessive local tax increases [4].
He said he personally favors removing the sales tax on gas and that this can be done without delaying road and bridge projects [4].

on_incumbent: Is the current officeholder. No statements by Alting about Baker were found in fetched sources [4].
plans: No general-election legislative agenda was found.
endorsements_finance: Endorsed by President Trump in March 2026 [5].
Wikipedia lists endorsements from Indiana Farm Bureau's AgELECT PAC and the NRA Political Victory Fund [6].
gaps: Search snippets reported that after the primary Alting said he felt he let some people down with his redistricting vote and that he was 'running against' public school teachers, a profession he respects; the source articles (Purdue Exponent, KPC News, Times syndication) returned 404/429 and could not be read.

A Hoosier Enquirer report said six Lafayette theft cases are linked to Alting, while it noted the court order refers to four Lafayette police case numbers; the J&C report read describes two incidents. The count is unconfirmed.
Search snippets (Wikipedia, citing a Reddit post) said he will not withdraw or resign; not verified.
His Monticello residence (reported by the J&C) versus the caucus's 'R-Lafayette' designation was not explained in available sources.
No fundraising totals found; the state campaign finance portal was not reviewed.
A Hoosier Enquirer report counted more theft cases than other outlets and quoted Senate leaders and his opponent; those details are not included because they could not be confirmed elsewhere.

candidates.summary: Natasha Baker is a public school Family and Consumer Sciences teacher from Battle Ground who has not held public office and who won the Democratic primary over Marlena Edmondson [7, 4, 6].
background: According to her campaign, she is a graduate of Harrison High School and Purdue University and a public school Family and Consumer Sciences teacher [7].
The Journal & Courier reported she is 34, lives in Battle Ground, and has held no prior public office [4].
path_to_ballot: Won the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary with 3,554 votes (62.1%) over Marlena Edmondson, per Wikipedia's results compilation [6].

items: She said she supports property-tax relief for seniors, veterans, and working families but does 'not support simply shifting the burden from property taxes to local income taxes,' arguing SB 1 reduced revenue for police, fire, roads, and libraries and citing Tippecanoe County public-safety staffing and school referendums [4].

She said she would support reinstating the gas tax to fund roads and bridges 'rather than permanently eliminating a transportation funding source,' and that property-tax relief is the bigger priority [4].
Her campaign says she is committed to protecting and strengthening public schools [7].
A podcast interview description said she discussed public schools needing 'real investment, not political games' [8].
Her campaign says she will push for policies that keep groceries, child care, and housing affordable and expand access to fresh, nutritious food [7].
A podcast interview description said she discussed gaps in health care access in rural and urban communities [8].

on_incumbent: No statements about the incumbent were found in sources that could be confirmed.
plans: Her campaign describes its theme as putting Hoosier families at the center of state policy [7].
endorsements_finance: iVoterGuide lists endorsements from the Indiana Reproductive Freedom PAC and MADVoters [9].
gaps: Search snippets said the Indiana Capital Chronicle voter guide lists her priorities as more funding for low-income child care vouchers, broader Medicaid coverage for preventive, mental health and addiction services, and expanded broadband; the guide returned 403.
Search snippets said WLFI reported she hosted a women-only introductory gun safety class and promotes 'common-sense' gun laws; the WLFI pages returned 404.
Primary totals differ: a KPC News snippet gave 3,355 votes and another snippet gave 62.1% to 32.9%; Wikipedia lists 3,554 (62.1%) to 2,045 (37.9%).
A search snippet quoted her saying voters will decide 'what kind of future we want for District 22'; not verified on a fetched page.
No fundraising totals found; the state campaign finance portal was not reviewed.
